title: After Wednesday's close: a scary morning, a calmer finish
text: Wednesday started badly. An inflation report came in hot, the U.S. proposed new tariffs, and AI chip stocks kept falling. At its worst, the Dow was down about 1,100 points. By the close it had climbed back to a small gain. The S&P 500 fund SPY ended down only 0.27% and the Nasdaq 100 fund QQQ down 0.69%. Chip makers still had a rough day: NVIDIA fell 3.9%. The market is closed Thursday for Thanksgiving and closes early, at 1 p.m. Eastern time, on Friday.

title: Inflation is speeding up again
text: The PCE report is the inflation number the Federal Reserve watches most. It showed prices were 3.8% higher in October than a year before, up from 3.6% in September. Core prices, which leave out food and energy because they jump around a lot, rose 3.3%. When inflation rises, the Fed may raise interest rates to cool things down. Higher rates can make stocks less attractive, especially fast growing tech companies.

title: New tariffs are proposed, not final
text: A tariff is a tax on goods that come from another country. The U.S. trade office proposed new tariffs of up to 20% on China, the European Union and 12 other economies. They are not in place yet. The earliest they could start is January, after public comments and hearings. Some items, like certain computer chips and medicines, would be left out. Markets often react to news like this before anything actually changes.

title: AI chip makers fell while some big AI users rose
text: NVIDIA dropped 3.9%, TSMC 2.0% and AMD 1.8%. On the other side, Meta rose 3.4%. Amazon fell 3.1% and Alphabet 2.1%, so the big AI users did not all move together. NVIDIA is now about 39% below its high of the past year. Its risk score is 6.5 out of 10. Lockheed Martin rose 2.2% and has the lowest risk score among single stocks on our list, at 2.9.

title: Lesson 67: What is a tariff?
text: A tariff is a tax a country charges on things brought in from other countries. Say a toy made overseas costs $10, and there is a 20% tariff. The company bringing it in pays $2 extra to the government. Often some of that cost gets passed on to shoppers through higher prices. Tariffs can help some local companies, because their foreign rivals become more expensive. But they can hurt companies that buy parts from abroad or sell a lot overseas. That is why stock prices can move just on the news that a tariff might be coming.

title: What this update covers
text: Prices, 52 week ranges, beta and company size come from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) as of Wednesday's close.
